# Transplantation

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Nephrology > Renal failure > Transplantation*

[Original Article Link](/library/gn0Fsg)

---

## Summary

Transplantation is the process of transferring an organ or part of an organ (known as a graft) from one donor to either themselves (<u>autologous</u> transplantation) or another recipient (allogeneic transplantation) or their genetically identical recipient (<u>isograft</u> transplantation). In addition to being subject to strict legal requirements, the donor and recipient must be histocompatible in allogeneic transplantations to minimize the risk of <u>transplant rejection</u>. Because the <u>major histocompatibility complex</u> (<u>MHC</u>) is only perfectly matched in isotransplantation (involving the transfer of genetically identical tissue, e.g., between <u>identical twins</u>), allogeneic transplantation subsequently requires <u>immunosuppressive therapy</u>. Close follow-up and infection prevention measures (e.g., <u>vaccination</u>) are required because of the risks of posttransplant infection and <u>graft rejection</u>

---

## Transplantation biology

### Transplant <u>immunology</u>




#### <u>Major histocompatibility complex</u> (<u>MHC</u>) and <u>human leukocyte antigen</u> (<u>HLA</u>)




* <u>HLA</u>: a <u>gene</u> cluster on <u>chromosome</u> 6 that codes for <u>MHC</u> molecules

* <u>MHC</u>: <u>proteins</u> present on the surface of all cells that display <u>antigenic</u> <u>peptides</u> as a normal physiological function so that they can be recognized by <u>T lymphocytes</u> as either self or non-self <u>antigens</u>

* Types of <u>MHC</u>

* The <u>HLA I</u> cluster codes for <u>class I MHC</u> molecules and consists of three <u>loci</u>: <u>HLA</u>-A, <u>HLA</u>-B, and <u>HLA</u>-C.

* The <u>HLA</u> II cluster codes for <u>class II MHC</u> molecules and also consists of three <u>loci</u>: <u>HLA-DR</u>, <u>HLA</u>-DP, and <u>HLA</u>-DQ.





See “<u>Major histocompatibility complex</u>” for more details.




#### Allorecognition




* Definition: recognition of a foreign <u>antigen</u> as a non-self <u>antigen</u> by a host

* Types of <u>allorecognition</u>

* Indirect <u>allorecognition</u>

* <u>HLA</u> molecules on an <u>allograft</u> are extremely different from those of the recipient and are thus treated as foreign <u>antigens</u> by the <u>antigen</u>-presenting cells of the recipient.

* The <u>antigens</u> are then broken down and presented by the <u>antigen</u>-presenting cells.

* Direct <u>allorecognition</u>: <u>HLA</u> molecules on the <u>allograft</u> are exceptionally strong <u>antigens</u> and can directly stimulate the <u>T cells</u> without being broken down and presented by the <u>antigen</u>-presenting cells of the recipient.

* Clinical importance: Activation of a particular <u>T cell</u> by a foreign <u>HLA</u> <u>peptide</u> results in clonal <u>proliferation</u> of that type of <u>T lymphocyte</u>, a process that is mediated by <u>IL-2</u> and leads to <u>acute rejection</u>.

* Activated cytotoxic (<u>CD<sub>8</sub></u>) <u>T cells</u> recognize other <u>HLA</u> class I molecules on all cells in the donor graft and cause <u>target cell</u> <u>death</u> by releasing molecules such as <u>perforin</u> and granulozyme.

* Activated helper (<u>CD<sub>4</sub></u>) <u>T cells</u> recognize <u>HLA</u> class II molecules on <u>dendritic cells</u> within the transplanted organ. 

* The activated helper <u>T cells</u> recruit recipient <u>macrophages</u> to the graft.

* The activated helper <u>T cells</u> help the <u>plasma cells</u> produce <u>alloantibodies</u> → damage the <u>target cell</u> directly or induce <u>antibody</u>-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity





### Prerequisites for organ matching




#### Crossmatching (transplantation)



* Recipient serum is examined for preformed <u>antibodies</u> (donor-specific antibodies) against donor T and <u>B lymphocytes</u> 

* A negative <u>crossmatch</u> against T and <u>B cells</u> indicates a lower risk of rejection reactions; therefore, transplantation may be performed.

* A negative <u>crossmatch</u> against <u>T cells</u> but a positive <u>crossmatch</u> against <u>B cells</u> indicates a higher risk of <u>acute rejection</u>, but transplantation may still be performed with a high level of caution.

* A positive <u>crossmatch</u> against donor T and <u>B lymphocytes</u> indicates a high risk of <u>hyperacute rejection</u>; therefore, the transplantation must not be performed.




#### ABO compatibility




* <u>Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation</u>

* ABO compatibility is preferred but incompatibility can be tolerated.

* ∼ 40% of allogeneic <u>stem cell</u> transplantations are performed despite <u>ABO incompatibility</u>.

* <u>Solid organ transplantation</u>: ABO compatibility is required.





> [!TIP]
> Rh compatibility is not required for <u>solid organ transplantation</u>. Both Rh compatibility and ABO compatibility are not essential for <u>hematopoietic stem cell transplantation</u>.




#### Histocompatibility




* Principle

* <u>MHC</u> matching at the <u>HLA-DR</u>, <u>HLA</u>-A, and <u>HLA</u>-B <u>loci</u>

* Matching of <u>HLA</u>-C, <u>HLA</u>-DP, and <u>HLA</u>-DQ is preferred but not always required.

* Coding of mismatch degree (<u>HLA-DR</u>, <u>HLA</u>-A, and <u>HLA</u>-B)

* 0: no mismatch

* 1: mismatch on either the paternal or maternal <u>chromosome</u>

* 2: mismatch on both the paternal and maternal <u>chromosome</u>

* 000: a complete match

* 222: a complete mismatch

* <u>Odds</u> of <u>histocompatibility</u>

* For a sibling, the <u>probability</u> that the patient has an <u>HLA</u> compatible sibling is 1 - (0.75)<sup>n</sup> (where n is the number of siblings).

* Between two randomly chosen, nonrelated individuals: 1 in 10,000





| Types of graft based on <u>histocompatibility</u> between donor and recipient |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type | Definition | Examples |
| Autograft | <br>* Graft originates from the recipient.<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Skin graft</u> (<u>split-skin</u> graft or full-thickness) for <u>skin transplantation</u><br><br>* Saphenous <u>vein</u> graft for <u>vascular bypass surgery</u><br><br>* Bone graft from the iliac crest for bone reconstruction<br><br>* <u>Semitendinosus</u> graft for cruciate <u>ligament</u> reconstruction<br><br>* Autotransfusion of blood<br><br>* <u>Hair</u> transplantation<br><br><br> |
| Isograft | <br>* Graft originates from a genetically identical person (<u>identical twin</u>).<br><br> | <br>* Various organ transplantations (e.g., <u>kidney</u>, <u>liver</u>, or <u>cornea</u>)<br><br> |
| Allograft | <br>* Graft originates from a genetically different person.<br><br> |  |
| Xenograft | <br>* Graft originates from a different species (e.g., pig).<br><br> | <br>* Porcine or bovine <u>heart valves</u><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> <u>Immunosuppressive therapy</u> is not required for <u>autograft</u> transplantation.

## Overview of pretransplant and posttransplant measures

### Pretransplant evaluation [[1]](/library/B51zmh0)[[2]](/library/A51R5h0)




* Consult multidisciplinary services for <u>pretransplant evaluation</u> and optimization.

* Infectious diseases: chronic infection management (e.g., <u>tuberculosis</u>)

* Social work: comprehensive psychosocial evaluation

* Other specialists: based on comorbid conditions (e.g., <u>morbid obesity</u>, <u>malnutrition</u>)

* Perform a <u>preoperative risk assessment</u> and coordinate <u>perioperative preparation</u> steps (e.g., <u>perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis</u>).





### Pretransplant infectious workup




* Screen both the donor and recipient for infections, including (at a minimum):

* <u>HIV</u>, <u>human T-cell lymphotropic virus</u>

* <u>Herpes simplex virus</u>, <u>varicella zoster virus</u>

* <u>Epstein-Barr virus</u>, <u>cytomegalovirus</u>

* <u>Viral hepatitis panel</u>

* <u>Rapid plasma reagin</u>

* <u>Toxoplasma gondii</u> <u>antibody</u>

* <u>Tuberculin skin test</u> or <u>interferon-γ release assay</u>

* Consider serological screening for <u>endemic</u> infections, e.g., <u>Leishmania</u>, <u>Trypanosoma cruzi</u>, <u>Strongyloides stercoralis</u>

* Ensure <u>immunization schedule</u> is completed.





### Posttransplant infectious workup[[3]](/library/v3YA4K)




* Monitoring

* <u>CMV</u> viral loads in blood monthly for a minimum of 12 months

* <u>EBV</u> viral loads in blood monthly for a minimum of 12 months

* In <u>kidney transplant</u> recipients: <u>BK virus</u> viral loads monthly for 6 months, then at 9 and 12 months

* Universal prophylaxis

* <u>PCP prophylaxis</u> with <u>trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole</u> for a minimum of 6–12 months

* <u>CMV</u> prophylaxis with <u>ganciclovir</u> or <u>valganciclovir</u> for 12–14 weeks

* Specific situations

* Recipients seronegative for <u>T. gondii</u> who receive a <u>heart transplant</u> from a seropositive individual: <u>pyrimethamine</u> with <u>folinic acid</u> for 6 months

* <u>Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation</u>

* <u>Acyclovir</u> for prophylaxis against <u>HSV</u> and <u>VZV</u>

* 12 months post-transplantation: <u>tetanus</u>, <u>diphtheria</u>, <u>H. influenzae</u>, <u>polio</u>, and <u>pneumococcal</u> <u>pneumonia</u> <u>vaccination</u>

* 24 months post-transplantation: <u>MMR</u>, <u>VZV</u>, and possibly <u>pertussis vaccination</u>





> [!TIP]
> Because the symptoms of <u>CMV infections</u> can appear similar to those of <u>transplant rejection</u>, differentiating between conditions can be difficult.




### Posttransplant immunosuppressive therapy [[4]](/library/mk1VoS0)




* Intense <u>immunosuppression</u> in the early postoperative period (3–6 months)

* To minimize drug toxicity, use low doses of multiple drugs rather than high doses of a few drugs.

* Avoid excessive <u>immunosuppression</u> that increases the risk of posttransplant infections and <u>posttransplant malignancy</u>.





#### Post <u>solid organ transplant</u>




* Phase 1: <u>induction therapy</u> using anti-<u>T-lymphocyte</u> <u>antibodies</u> 

* Nondepleting <u>antibodies</u> (monoclonal): <u>basiliximab</u>

* <u>Lymphocyte</u>-depleting <u>antibodies</u> (polyclonal): thymoglobulin

* Phase 2: <u>maintenance therapy</u>. Commonly a triple-drug regimen consisting of:

* <u>Glucocorticoids</u>

* <u>Calcineurin inhibitor</u> (e.g., <u>cyclosporine</u>, <u>tacrolimus</u>)

* Antiproliferative agents (e.g., <u>azathioprine</u>, <u>mycophenolate mofetil</u>, <u>sirolimus</u>)





#### Post <u>allogeneic stem cell transplant</u>




See “Prevention” in “<u>Graft-versus-host disease</u>.”




> [!TIP]
> <u>Immunosuppressive therapy</u> is a balancing act: Too much <u>immunosuppression</u>, and the risk of infection increases; too little, and the risk of rejection increases.

---

## Solid organ transplantation

### General principles [[2]](/library/A51R5h0)




* Long-term management includes monitoring of:

* <u>Allograft</u> function

* <u>Adverse effects of immunosuppressants</u>

* Posttransplant infections

* Transplant centers typically guide posttransplant management for 3–12 months.

* Consider a broad differential diagnosis and consult specialists for patients with complications (e.g., <u>graft rejection</u>, posttransplant infections).





### Living donors




* Advantages

* Donor is usually healthy, which reduces the risk of complications for both donor and recipient.

* Preoperative and perioperative immunomodulation is possible in the recipient.

* Short <u>cold ischemia time</u>

* Minimal waiting time





* Nonvital organs and tissues (e.g., <u>kidney</u> or <u>bone marrow</u>) can be acquired from living donors.

* The organ is retrieved from a living donor (usually a relative with a compatible blood type) at the time of the transplant <u>surgery</u>.

* When there is no relative with blood type compatibility, a donor may engage in a swap transplantation with a nonrelated donor.

* Prior to donation, donors must give full <u>informed consent</u>.

* Donors may select the recipient of their donation.

* Donors may not be paid for their donation, but can be reimbursed for associated costs (e.g., travel, food, lost wages).

* Disadvantages: increased risk of <u>morbidity</u> and mortality in the donor





### Deceased and dying donors




<u>Organ donation</u> can save lives, and doctors play an important role in the <u>organ donation</u> system. Doctors should always honor their patients' end-of-life wishes and provide the best possible care, but they should also recognize the medical and social benefits of <u>organ donation</u>. When treating a dying patient, it is therefore important to initiate conversations with the patient and their family about the potential for <u>organ donation</u>. Due to the ethical concerns associated with <u>organ donation</u>, there are several procedures in place to protect the interests of the patient while expanding the practice of donation.




#### Legal and organizational aspects




* An individual may register to become an organ donor (e.g., in a state donor registry) and can revoke this decision at any time.

* Donors may specify the solid organs they wish to donate (e.g., <u>heart</u>, two <u>lungs</u>, two <u>kidneys</u>, <u>pancreas</u>, <u>liver</u>).

* The organ is retrieved from a donor after <u>brain</u>-<u>death</u> (DBD) or a donor after circulatory <u>death</u> (DCD).

* Deceased patients who have not specifically declined to become donors (e.g., in an <u>advance directive</u>) may be considered if consent is obtained from the <u>next of kin</u>.

* Dying patients (e.g, terminally ill, in <u>palliative care</u>) who have not previously opted-in to the donation system may also be considered for <u>organ donation</u>.

* To avoid any <u>conflict of interest</u>, the decision to end life-sustaining care is always made by a medical team that is independent of the transplant team.

* If the individual is a donor candidate and did not explicitly decline to donate organs (e.g., in a <u>living will</u>) the hospital notifies the local Organ Procurement Organization (OPO).

* Factors that the OPO will consider:

* Is there an <u>organ donation</u> plan?

* If no such plan exists, did the deceased declare their intention to donate organs (e.g., by registering in the state organ donor registry)?

* If the patient did not declare their intention to donate organs, the OPO discusses the possibility of donation with the patient's <u>next of kin</u>.

* Is the patient a suitable candidate for donation?





#### Organ assessment and matching




* The Organ Procurement and Transplant Network (OPTN) is a national system that links all professionals involved in <u>organ donation</u> and transplantation (e.g., OPOs, transplant centers, <u>histocompatibility</u> laboratories).

* It is administered by the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS), a private nonprofit organization contracted by the federal government.

* The UNOS manages the national transplant waiting list and works with OPOs to match donors with recipients.

* Guidelines for matching include donor compatibility, medical utility, geography, and survival benefit of the transplant.

* The following are the expected waiting periods for new transplant candidates:

* <u>Kidney</u>: 5 years

* <u>Liver</u>: 11 months

* <u>Heart</u>: 4 months

* <u>Lung</u>: 4 months

* <u>Pancreas</u>: 2 years

* <u>Kidney</u>/<u>pancreas</u>: 1.5 years

* Contraindications for the acceptance of organs include:  [[5]](/library/obX0u9)[[6]](/library/KbXUu9)

* Terminal malignancies and/or malignancies with a high risk of transmission, such as <u>melanomas</u> and <u>choriocarcinomas</u>

* Untreated fungal, bacterial, or viral <u>sepsis</u>

* Transmissible spongiform <u>encephalopathies</u> (e.g., <u>Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease</u>)

* <u>Cardiac arrest</u> occurring before <u>brain death</u>

* Poor organ function or prolonged organ <u>ischemia</u>

* Circumstances under which organ transplants can be accepted include:

* For <u>HIV</u>-positive recipients: donor <u>HIV infection</u>  [[7]](/library/uIYpeq)[[8]](/library/E3Y84K)

* For <u>hepatitis C</u>-positive recipients: donor <u>hepatitis C</u> infection

* For <u>HBsAg</u>-positive recipients or recipients with <u>HBV</u> <u>immunity</u>: donor <u>hepatitis B</u> infection

* Low-grade, localized tumors without evidence of <u>metastasis</u> at the <u>time of death</u>

* History of <u>malignancy</u> with a disease-free duration > 5 years

* <u>Hypertension</u>

* <u>Diabetes</u>

* Advanced age (if organ function is preserved)





### Organ preservation




* Hypothermic solutions

* Extracellular solutions (e.g., Bretschneider solution): ↑ Na<sup>+</sup>, ↓ <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>

* Intracellular solutions (e.g., University of Wisconsin solution, St. Thomas <u>cardioplegia</u> solution): ↓ Na<sup>+</sup>, ↑ <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>

* <u>Ischemic</u> times

* Warm ischemia time: time from the <u>withdrawal of life support</u> in the donor to the initiation of cold organ preservation

* Cold ischemia time: time from the initiation of cold organ preservation to the warming of the organ within the recipient following the restoration of blood <u>perfusion</u>





> [!TIP]
> A prolonged <u>ischemic</u> time increases the risk of organ dysfunction in the posttransplant period.




### Transplantation sites




| Overview of organ transplantation sites |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Description | Examples |
| <u>Orthotopic</u> | <br><br>* The graft is placed in the normal <u>anatomical position</u>.<br><br>* The diseased or nonfunctional organ being replaced is removed.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Heart transplantation</u><br><br>* <u>Liver transplantation</u><br><br><br> |
| Heterotopic | <br><br>* The graft is placed in a site other than the normal <u>anatomical position</u>.<br><br>* The nonfunctional organ is usually left in place.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Kidney transplantation</u><br><br>* <u>Pancreas</u> transplantation<br><br><br> |
| Paratopic | <br>* The donor organ is placed close to the normal <u>anatomical position</u>.<br><br> | <br>* <u>Pancreas</u> transplantation<br><br> |

## Renal transplantation

### Overview




* Number of procedures: 23,401 in 2019 in the US

* Indication: patients with <u>end-stage renal disease</u> (<u>CKD</u> 5)

* Contraindications

* Absolute

* Unsuitable vascular anatomy

* Aortobifemoral bypass or an aortoiliac <u>stent</u> graft that extends to both <u>external iliac arteries</u>

* Circumferential calcification of the iliac vessels

* <u>Thrombosis</u> of iliac <u>vein</u> and <u>inferior vena cava</u>

* Active infection (e.g., <u>tuberculosis</u>, invasive <u>fungal infections</u>, <u>osteomyelitis</u>)

* <u>Malignancy</u> in the past 2 years

* <u>BMI</u> ≥ 50 kg/m<sup>2</sup>

* Active <u>alcohol</u> or substance use (except tobacco)

* Lack of adequate social support (e.g., patient in a <u>nursing home</u>, homeless patient)

* Relative

* Age < 1 year or > 75 years

* Diseases of the <u>lower urinary tract</u>

* Specific contraindications for living donors

* <u>Pregnancy</u>

* Psychiatric diseases or psychosocial problems

* Diseases potentially leading to <u>kidney</u> damage 

* <u>Proteinuria</u> > 300 mg/24 h

* <u>Hypertension</u> that does not respond to treatment

* <u>Diabetes mellitus</u>

* Technique

* The left <u>kidney</u> is preferred in living-donor <u>kidney transplantations</u> because it has a longer <u>renal vein</u>.

* <u>Kidney transplants</u> are transplanted heterotopically in the iliac fossa since this position holds several advantages over <u>orthotopic</u> implantation.

* The transplanted <u>kidney</u> can be more easily palpated, biopsied, and evaluated via <u>ultrasound</u>.

* Vascular <u>anastomosis</u> with the inguinal <u>arteries</u> is easier.

* Distance between the <u>ureter</u> and <u>bladder</u> is shorter.





> [!TIP]
> Two healthy, fully functioning <u>kidneys</u> are an essential requirement for <u>kidney</u> donation by a living donor.




> [!TIP]
> The left <u>kidney</u> is preferred for living-donor transplantation as it has a longer <u>renal vein</u>.




### Complications of renal transplantation [[9]](/library/Mk1MoS0)[[10]](/library/Km1Ugh0)




The most important complications are listed. Timelines are estimates.




#### Any time post-transplant




* Posttransplant infections

* <u>Graft rejection</u>, e.g., <u>acute rejection</u>: 

* ↑ Blood pressure and <u>kidney function</u> lab values

* ↓ Urine output

* <u>Adverse effects of immunosuppressants</u> (e.g., <u>calcineurin</u>-induced <u>nephrotoxicity</u>)

* Recurrence of primary disease  [[11]](/library/Cm1q3h0)





#### Acute postoperative (< 1 week)




* <u>Acute tubular necrosis</u>

* Urinary leakage  [[12]](/library/om10gh0)

* Clinical features: increased postoperative drain output, graft <u>pain</u> and/or swelling, <u>fever</u>, <u>urinoma</u>

* Diagnostics: abdominal imaging , biochemical analysis of drainage fluid

* <u>Renal vein thrombosis</u> (rare and serious)

* Clinical features: <u>oliguria</u>, <u>hematuria</u>, graft <u>pain</u>/swelling

* Diagnostics: <u>Doppler ultrasound</u>

* Treatment: urgent surgical intervention (e.g., thrombectomy, <u>nephrectomy</u>)





#### Early (1–12 weeks)




* <u>Urinary tract obstruction</u> (acute)

* Etiology: extraluminal compression (e.g., <u>hematoma</u>), <u>edema</u>, <u>thrombus</u>, kinking of the <u>anastomosis</u>

* Clinical features: <u>renal colic</u>, <u>hematuria</u>, <u>oliguria</u>

* <u>Lymphocele</u>

* Clinical features: often asymptomatic or nonspecific symptoms

* Diagnostics: biochemical analysis and microscopy of the fluid collection

* <u>Renal artery</u> <u>thrombosis</u> (rare and serious)





#### Late (> 12 weeks)




* <u>Renal artery stenosis</u>: most common vascular complication (onset is often ∼ 6 months post-transplant) [[13]](/library/ym1dRh0)

* Etiology: anastomotic failure, <u>atheroma</u>, immune-mediated

* Clinical features: renal dysfunction, <u>hypertension</u>

* Diagnostics: <u>ultrasound</u>, CT or <u>MR angiography</u>

* <u>Urinary tract obstruction</u> (subacute or chronic) [[14]](/library/Lm1wTh0)

* Etiology: <u>fibrosis</u> of the <u>ureter</u>

* Clinical features: <u>hypertension</u>; often asymptomatic

* <u>Posttransplant malignancy</u> (e.g., <u>renal cell carcinoma</u>)





### Posttransplant care [[15]](/library/Am1RRh0)




* Within 24 hours of transplant, one or more dialysis treatments may be required in patients with any of the following:

* Delayed graft function  [[16]](/library/_m15Rh0)

* <u>Indications for renal replacement therapy</u> similar to nontransplant patients (e.g., refractory <u>hyperkalemia</u>, <u>pulmonary edema</u>)

* Long-term management

* Serial monitoring of <u>renal function tests</u> (e.g., serum <u>creatinine</u>, urine protein)

* See “<u>Posttransplant immunosuppressive therapy</u>.”

* See “Prevention of posttransplant infections.”





### Diagnostic algorithm for renal dysfunction following <u>renal transplantation</u>



1. * Consider <u>prerenal</u> causes of <u>acute renal failure</u>.

* In hypotensive or <u>normotensive</u> patients, measure the <u>BUN</u>:<u>creatinine</u> <u>ratio</u> to rule out <u>dehydration</u>.

* In hypertensive patients, consider <u>renal artery stenosis</u> and perform <u>Doppler ultrasonography</u>.
2. * Measure urine protein and order a <u>dipstick</u> urine test for <u>hematuria</u>.

* <u>Hematuria</u> or <u>proteinuria</u>: <u>renal biopsy</u>

* No <u>hematuria</u> or <u>proteinuria</u>

* If the patient is not taking <u>anticalcineurins</u>: <u>renal biopsy</u>

* If the patient is taking <u>anticalcineurins</u>: measure serum <u>anticalcineurin</u> levels

* ↑ <u>Anticalcineurin</u> levels: Reduce <u>anticalcineurin</u> dose and remeasure <u>creatinine</u>.

* Unchanged <u>anticalcineurin</u> levels (i.e., within the target range): Perform <u>renal and bladder ultrasound</u> to rule out obstruction.

* ↓ <u>Anticalcineurin</u> levels: Carry out a <u>renal biopsy</u>.




### Prognosis




The graft functions stays functional for ∼ 14 years, longer if received from a living donor.




| Overview of survival rates after <u>kidney transplantation</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | 1-year survival rate | 2-year survival rate | 5-year survival rate |
| Cadaveric graft | 88% | 81% | 71% |
| Graft from living donor | 94% | 93% | 84% |





> [!TIP]
> <u>Renal transplantation</u> has a better prognosis than dialysis in <u>end-stage renal disease</u>.

---

## Liver transplantation

### Overview [[17]](/library/XSa9yP)




* Number of procedures: 8,896 in 2019 in the US

* Indications

* <u>Hepatocellular carcinoma</u> without <u>metastatic</u> disease and with either one lesion measuring ≤ 5 cm or three lesions each measuring ≤ 3 cm

* <u>Fulminant hepatic failure</u>

* <u>Decompensated cirrhosis</u> with a <u>MELD score</u> ≥ 15 

* <u>Hepatitis C</u>

* Alcoholic <u>cirrhosis</u>

* <u>Primary biliary cirrhosis</u>

* <u>Primary sclerosing cholangitis</u>

* <u>Biliary atresia</u>

* <u>Hemochromatosis</u>

* <u>α1-antitrypsin deficiency</u>

* <u>Wilson disease</u>

* Severe metabolic dysfunction due to <u>liver</u>-related diseases with systemic manifestations (e.g., <u>Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I</u>, <u>glycogen storage disorders</u> types I, III, IV)

* Contraindications

* <u>MELD score</u> < 15

* <u>Alcohol</u> or drug use disorder

* <u>Hepatocellular carcinoma</u> with <u>metastatic</u> spread

* Intrahepatic cholangiosarcoma

* Severe cardiac or pulmonary disease

* <u>AIDS</u>  [[17]](/library/XSa9yP)

* Extrahepatic <u>malignancy</u>

* Uncontrolled <u>sepsis</u>

* <u>Fulminant hepatic failure</u> with a sustained <u>ICP</u> > 50 mm Hg or <u>CPP</u> < 40 mm Hg

* Lack of adequate social support

* Technique: <u>orthotopic</u> transplantation

* Transfer of the entire organ from a <u>brain</u>-dead donor (BDD)

* Split-<u>liver</u> transplantation from a living donor or BDD





### Complications of liver transplantation [[18]](/library/3O1SHS0)[[19]](/library/RO1lHS0)[[20]](/library/f51kjh0)




The most important complications are listed. Timelines are estimates.




#### Vascular complications [[21]](/library/U51bjh0)




* <u>Postoperative hemorrhage</u>

* Hepatic artery thrombosis: most common vascular complication

* Clinical features: elevated <u>hepatocellular enzymes</u>, <u>fever</u>, graft <u>necrosis</u>

* Sequela: biliary complications, high <u>incidence</u> of graft failure

* Diagnostics: <u>Doppler ultrasound</u> or CT abdomen

* Treatment: thrombectomy, <u>stenting</u>, <u>thrombolysis</u>, retransplantation

* <u>Portal vein thrombosis</u>

* Hepatic <u>artery</u> stenosis: Median onset ∼ 3 months post-transplant [[19]](/library/RO1lHS0)





#### Biliary complications [[22]](/library/T516jh0)




* Biliary leakage: typically occurs within 6 months of transplantation

* Etiology: vascular complications, dehiscence of <u>anastomosis</u>, <u>T-tube</u> removal

* Clinical features: <u>fever</u>, <u>signs of peritonitis</u>

* Diagnostics: <u>ERCP</u>

* <u>Biliary stricture</u> (anastomotic and nonanastomotic)

* <u>Bile duct obstruction</u>

* <u>Biloma</u>





#### Other complications




* Posttransplant infections

* <u>Graft rejection</u> [[23]](/library/z1Wrj40)

* <u>Acute cellular rejection</u>

* Typically occurs within one month of transplantation

* <u>Incidence</u>: 10–30% of patients who take <u>immunosuppressive therapy</u>

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>: elevation of <u>AST</u>/<u>ALT</u>, <u>ALP</u>, <u>GGT</u>, <u>bilirubin</u>

* Definitive diagnosis: graft <u>biopsy</u> showing <u>eosinophil</u>, <u>lymphocyte</u>, and/or <u>neutrophil</u> infiltration in <u>portal tracts</u> and inflammation of <u>bile</u> ducts and venous <u>endothelium</u>

* Prognosis: responds well to treatment with <u>steroids</u>

* <u>Chronic rejection</u>

* Typically occurs months to years after transplantation

* Diagnostics: graft <u>biopsy</u> showing obliterative arteriopathy and ductopenia

* Prognosis: may result in graft loss and possibly <u>death</u>

* <u>Adverse effects of immunosuppressants</u>

* <u>Posttransplant malignancy</u>

* Recurrence of primary disease





### Diagnostic algorithm in the case of clinical or laboratory features of hepatic dysfunction




* < 6 months post-transplant: <u>duplex ultrasonography</u> to identify biliary or vascular pathology

* No evidence of biliary dilation or vascular pathology: <u>liver biopsy</u>

* Evidence of biliary dilation: <u>ERCP</u> or <u>percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography</u>

* > 6 months post-transplant: <u>liver biopsy</u>





### Posttransplant care




* Serial monitoring of <u>liver function</u> tests, including <u>ALP</u>

* See “<u>Posttransplant immunosuppressive therapy</u>.”

* See “Prevention of posttransplant infections.”





### Prognosis




* High <u>mortality rate</u> within first postoperative year due to the greatest <u>immunosuppression</u> and subsequent infections

* <u>5-year survival rate</u>: ∼ 80%

* Very good prognosis for pediatric <u>liver transplantation</u>

---

## Heart transplantation

### Overview [[24]](/library/hB0c0i)[[25]](/library/3B0S0i)[[26]](/library/WSaPAP)




* Number of procedures: 3552 in 2019 in the US

* Indications

* <u>End-stage heart failure</u> (<u>NYHA class</u> IV) and an <u>ejection fraction</u> < 20% with no other viable treatment option

* Otherwise untreatable, intractable, life-threatening <u>ventricular arrhythmias</u>

* <u>Hypoplastic left heart syndrome</u>

* Severe <u>Ebstein anomaly</u>

* <u>Pulmonary atresia</u>

* <u>Heterotaxy</u> lesions

* Contraindications

* <u>Absolute contraindications</u>

* <u>AIDS</u> with recurrent <u>opportunistic infections</u>

* <u>Malignancy</u> within the past 5 years

* <u>Obstructive lung disease</u> with an <u>FEV<sub>1</sub></u> < 1 L/min

* <u>Pulmonary hypertension</u>

* <u>Pulmonary artery systolic pressure</u> > 60 mm Hg

* Mean transpulmonary gradient > 15 mm Hg

* <u>Pulmonary vascular resistance</u> > 6 <u>Wood units</u>

* Active <u>SLE</u>, <u>sarcoidosis</u>, or <u>amyloidosis</u> with multisystem involvement

* <u>ESRD</u> or irreversible hepatic failure if <u>cardiac transplantation</u> alone is being considered

* <u>Relative contraindications</u>

* Any active infection (except device-related infection in individuals with <u>ventricular assist devices</u>)

* Age > 72 years

* <u>FEV<sub>1</sub></u> < 40% of the normal value

* <u>Pulmonary infarction</u> in the past 6–8 weeks

* <u>Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia</u> in the last 100 days

* <u>Chronic renal failure</u> (<u>creatinine</u> > 2.5 mg/dL)

* Hepatic dysfunction (<u>bilirubin</u> > 2.5 mg/dL, serum <u>transaminase</u> more than 3 times the upper limit, or <u>INR</u> > 1.5 without <u>warfarin</u>)

* Active <u>peptic ulcer disease</u>

* Severe <u>malnutrition</u> (<u>BMI</u> < 18 kg/m<sup>2</sup>)

* <u>Morbid obesity</u> (<u>BMI</u> > 35 kg/m<sup>2</sup>)

* Severe <u>diabetes mellitus</u>

* Uncontrolled <u>hypertension</u>

* Severe <u>peripheral vascular disease</u>

* <u>Abdominal aortic aneurysm</u> > 6 cm

* <u>Symptomatic carotid stenosis</u>

* Irreversible neurological disease

* Mental illness

* Drug, tobacco, or <u>alcohol</u> consumption in the past 6 months

* Technique: A graft from a deceased donor is transplanted orthotopically.
1. * Midline <u>sternotomy</u>
2. * Systemic anticoagulation and <u>cardiopulmonary bypass</u> with <u>therapeutic hypothermia</u>
3. * The aorta is crossclamped and the recipient <u>heart</u> is excised at the level of the mid-<u>atrium</u>, leaving the <u>pulmonary veins</u> and vena cava intact.
4. * Creation of an atrial cuff in the donor <u>heart</u>
5. * <u>Anastomosis</u> of the atrial cuff first with the remnant of the recipient's <u>left atrium</u>, then the <u>right atrium</u>.
6. * <u>Anastomosis</u> of the <u>pulmonary artery</u> and aorta
7. * Closure of the midline <u>sternotomy</u>, rewarming the patient, and <u>weaning</u> off of <u>cardiopulmonary bypass</u>





### Complications




* Posttransplant infections

* <u>Graft rejection</u> 

* Hyperacute and accelerated rejection → <u>cardiogenic shock</u>

* <u>Acute rejection</u> → <u>arrhythmias</u>, <u>heart failure</u>

* <u>Chronic rejection</u> → acquired transplant vasculopathy → accelerated <u>coronary artery disease</u> → <u>angina</u>, low <u>stress</u> tolerance

* <u>Pulmonary hypertension</u> → <u>right heart failure</u>





### Posttransplant care




* Surveillance <u>endomyocardial biopsies</u> to identify rejection reactions

* See “<u>Posttransplant immunosuppressive therapy</u>.”

* See “Prevention of posttransplant infections.”





### Prognosis




| Overview of survival rates after <u>heart transplantation</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | 1-year survival rate | 3-year survival rate | <u>5-year survival rate</u> |
| Primary transplants | <br>* 87%<br><br> | <br>* 79%<br><br> | <br>* 72%<br><br> |
| Retransplants | <br>* 82%<br><br> | <br>* 67%<br><br> | <br>* 58%<br><br> |

---

## Lung transplantation

### Overview [[27]](/library/nIY7Wq)




* Number of procedures: 2714 in 2019 in the US

* Indication: patients with advanced <u>lung</u> disease refractory to maximal medical or surgical therapy, disabling symptoms during <u>activities of daily living</u>, and risk of <u>death</u> > 50% over the next 2 years

* <u>COPD</u>

* <u>Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis</u>

* Genetic disorders such as <u>CF</u> and <u>α1-antitrypsin deficiency</u>

* <u>Idiopathic</u> <u>pulmonary arterial hypertension</u> (IPAH)

* <u>Sarcoidosis</u>

* <u>Lymphangioleiomyomatosis</u>

* Pulmonary <u>Langerhans cell histiocytosis</u>

* Contraindications

* Absolute

* <u>Malignancy</u> in the past 2 years

* Chronic advanced illnesses (e.g., <u>heart</u>, renal, or hepatic insufficiency)

* Uncontrolled or untreatable pulmonary or extrapulmonary infection

* Poor cardiac function

* Acute medical conditions, such as <u>sepsis</u>, <u>myocardial infarction</u>, or <u>liver</u> failure

* Uncorrectable <u>bleeding diathesis</u>

* <u>HIV infection</u> (unless the viral load is undetectable)

* Significant <u>chest wall</u> or spinal deformity

* <u>BMI</u> ≥ 35

* History of nonadherence to medical therapy

* Psychiatric conditions or psychosocial problems

* Lack of adequate social support

* Severely limited functional status with poor <u>rehabilitation</u> potential

* Active <u>alcohol</u>, tobacco, or <u>substance use disorder</u>

* Relative

* Age > 75 years

* <u>BMI</u> 30–35

* Progressive or severe <u>malnutrition</u>

* Severe, symptomatic <u>osteoporosis</u>

* Prior chest <u>surgery</u> with <u>lung</u> resection

* Infection with highly resistant or <u>virulent</u> bacteria, fungi, and/or certain strains of <u>mycobacteria</u>

* Ongoing <u>HBV</u>, <u>HCV</u>, or <u>TB</u> infections

* Techniques: A graft from a deceased donor is transplanted orthotopically.

* Bilateral <u>orthotopic</u> <u>lung transplantation</u> (BOLT) is the preferred procedure.

* In a single-<u>lung transplant</u>, the right <u>lung</u> or the <u>lung</u> with the worse <u>pulmonary function</u> is chosen for replacement.

* Types of <u>lung transplant</u>

* Lobe [[28]](/library/pIYLdq)

* Single-<u>lung</u>

* Double-<u>lung</u>

* <u>Heart</u>-<u>lung</u>





### Complications of lung transplantation [[29]](/library/sl1tyS0)




The most important complications are listed. Timelines are estimates.




#### Any time post-transplant




##### <u>Graft rejection</u>




* Acute lung transplant rejection (ALTR) [[30]](/library/beWHx40)

* Definition: an acute complication, occurring within the first year of transplantation, in which the recipient's <u>T-lymphocytes</u> or <u>antibodies</u> attack <u>antigens</u> in the donated <u>lung</u>

* Clinical features

* Usually asymptomatic or nonspecific symptoms (e.g., <u>cough</u>, <u>shortness of breath</u>, <u>tachypnea</u>, <u>fever</u>, <u>hypoxemia</u>, <u>crackles</u> on <u>auscultation</u>)

* Severe cases: acute <u>respiratory distress</u>

* Diagnostics

* Blood test: <u>donor-specific antibodies</u> (<u>DSA</u>) in case of <u>antibody</u>-mediated rejection

* <u>Chest x-ray</u>: perihilar opacities, <u>interstitial</u> <u>edema</u>, <u>pleural effusion</u>

* <u>CT scan</u>: <u>ground-glass opacities</u>, septal thickening, volume loss, <u>pleural effusion</u>

* <u>Spirometry</u>: ↓ <u>FEV<sub>1</sub></u> and/or ↓ <u>FVC</u>

* <u>Bronchoscopy</u> with <u>bronchoalveolar lavage</u> (<u>BAL</u>) and transbronchial <u>biopsy</u>

* <u>Bronchoscopy</u> with <u>BAL</u>: to help differentiate ALTR from bronchial stenosis and infection

* Transbronchial <u>biopsy</u> (<u>gold standard</u>): <u>lymphocytic</u> perivascular or peribronchial infiltrates

* Differential diagnoses

* Posttransplant infections

* Bronchial stenosis

* <u>Tracheobronchomalacia</u>

* <u>Exophytic</u> <u>granulation tissue</u>

* <u>Chronic lung allograft dysfunction</u>

* <u>Thromboembolism</u>

* Recurrence of primary disease

* Treatment: <u>plasmapheresis</u> and/or <u>immunosuppression</u>

* Chronic lung allograft dysfunction (<u>CLAD</u>) [[31]](/library/3eWSA40)

* Definition: a progressive decline in <u>lung function</u> more than a year after transplantation that persists for longer than 3 weeks

* <u>Phenotypes</u>: <u>bronchiolitis obliterans</u> syndrome (most common) and restrictive <u>allograft</u> syndrome

* Clinical features: asymptomatic or nonspecific symptoms (e.g., <u>dyspnea</u>, nonproductive <u>cough</u>, <u>tachypnea</u>, <u>hypoxemia</u>, <u>crackles</u> on <u>auscultation</u>)

* Diagnostics: ≥ 20% ↓ in <u>FEV1</u> or <u>FVC</u> from posttransplant baseline for at least 3 weeks

* Management: <u>azithromycin</u>, <u>immunosuppression</u>, retransplantation





##### Other




* Posttransplant infections;  (especially <u>pneumonia</u>)

* <u>Adverse effects of immunosuppressants</u>

* Recurrence of primary disease





#### Early (< 4 weeks)




* <u>Primary graft dysfunction</u> [[32]](/library/P51W4h0)

* Definition: <u>acute lung injury</u> within 72 hours of transplantation

* Etiology: <u>ischemia-reperfusion injury</u>, <u>mechanical ventilation</u>

* <u>Pleural effusions</u>: <u>hemothorax</u>, <u>chylothorax</u>, <u>empyema</u>

* <u>Venous thromboembolism</u>

* Pulmonary vascular stenosis: <u>pulmonary artery</u> (more common) and <u>pulmonary vein</u>

* Etiology: kinking of the <u>anastomosis</u>, donor anatomy, <u>thrombosis</u>

* Clinical features: <u>pulmonary edema</u>, <u>hypoxemia</u>

* Diagnostics: <u>CTA</u> chest, <u>transesophageal echocardiogram</u>

* <u>Pneumothorax</u>

* Nerve injury

* Bronchial <u>necrosis</u> and dehiscence [[33]](/library/k51m4h0)

* Clinical features: <u>dyspnea</u>, failed <u>trial of spontaneous breathing</u>, <u>subcutaneous emphysema</u>, <u>pneumomediastinum</u>

* Diagnostics: <u>bronchoscopy</u>





#### Late (> 4 weeks) [[33]](/library/k51m4h0)




<u>Signs of airway obstruction</u> and <u>post-obstructive pneumonia</u> are common manifestations of late <u>lung transplant</u> complications.




* Bronchial stenosis: most common <u>airway</u> complication following <u>lung transplantation</u>  [[33]](/library/k51m4h0)

* <u>Exophytic</u> <u>granulation tissue</u>

* Etiology: excess inflammatory response, <u>ischemia</u>, trauma from therapeutic interventions (e.g., <u>stent</u>)

* Diagnostics: abnormal <u>spirometry</u>

* <u>Tracheobronchomalacia</u>

* <u>Fistulae</u>: e.g., bronchopleural, bronchovascular, bronchomediastinal

* Clinical features: vary based on the type of <u>fistula</u>

* Diagnostics: CT chest, <u>bronchoscopy</u>

* <u>Chronic lung allograft dysfunction</u> (e.g., <u>bronchiolitis obliterans</u>)

* Post-transplant <u>malignancy</u>





### Post-transplant care




* <u>Pulmonary rehabilitation</u>

* Serial monitoring of <u>lung function tests</u> (e.g., <u>PFT</u>, <u>CT scan</u> of the chest, <u>bronchoscopy</u>)

* See “<u>Post-transplant immunosuppressive therapy</u>.”

* See “Prevention of post-transplant infections.”





### Prognosis




* Median survival for all adult recipients: 5.7 years

* 1-year survival rate: 78%

* <u>5-year survival rate</u>: 51%

---

## Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation

### <u>Hematopoietic stem cell</u>




* A <u>stem cell</u> that can give rise to all lines of blood cells via <u>hematopoiesis</u>.

* Excellent regenerative capacity

* Ability of <u>homing</u> to the <u>bone marrow</u> following intravenous injections





| Overview of <u>hematopoietic stem cell</u> grafts |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Bone marrow transplant | Peripheral blood stem cell transplant | Umbilical cord blood transplant |
| Source | <br>* <u>Bone marrow aspiration</u> from the <u>posterior</u> superior iliac <u>spine</u><br><br> | <br>* Pheresis of peripheral blood after administering a myeloid growth factor (e.g., <u>G-CSF</u>, <u>GM-CSF</u>) or <u>plerixafor</u> (a <u>CXCR4</u> <u>antagonist</u>) for 4–5 days<br><br> | <br>* <u>Umbilical cord</u> blood that is collected at the time of delivery and stored in <u>stem cell</u> banks<br><br> |
| Risk of <u>graft-vs-host disease</u>(<u>GvHD</u>) | <br>* Lowest<br><br> | <br>* Highest<br><br> | <br>* Low<br><br> |
| Engraftment | <br>* By 3 weeks<br><br> | <br>* By 2 weeks<br><br> | <br>* By 4 weeks<br><br> |





### Types of <u>hematopoietic stem cell transplantation</u> (<u>HSCT</u>)




| <u>Autologous</u> vs. <u>allogeneic stem cell transplantation</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Autologous stem cell transplantation | Allogeneic stem cell transplantation |
| Definition | <br>* Removal and storage of a patient's own <u>hematopoietic stem cells</u>, which are retransfused back to the patient after high-dose <u>myeloablative</u> <u>chemotherapy</u><br><br> | <br>* Transfer of <u>hematopoietic stem cells</u> of a sibling or unrelated donor to a recipient<br><br> |
| <br>Indications [[34]](/library/dSaoAP) | <br><br>* <u>Germ cell tumors</u>, <u>soft tissue sarcoma</u>: to allow the administration of higher doses of <u>antineoplastic therapy</u><br><br>* <u>Multiple myeloma</u><br><br>* <u>Lymphoma</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Leukemia</u> (e.g., <u>acute lymphoblastic leukemia</u>)<br><br>* To replace abnormal but nonmalignant cells of the lymphohematopoietic system in conditions such as:<br><br>* <u>Severe combined immunodeficiency</u><br><br>* <u>Aplastic anemia</u><br><br>* <u>Thalassemia</u><br><br>* Relapse of <u>lymphoma</u> or <u>multiple myeloma</u> following <u>autologous stem cell transplantation</u><br><br><br> |
| Preferred graft source | <br>* <u>Bone marrow transplant</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Peripheral blood stem cell transplant</u><br><br> |
| Advantages | <br><br>* Low risk of <u>GvHD</u> and late-onset posttransplant infections<br><br>* Low risk of <u>graft rejection</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Graft-versus-tumor effect: Donor <u>T lymphocytes</u> attack malignant <u>hematopoietic stem cells</u> of the recipient that remain after <u>high-dose chemotherapy</u>.<br><br>* Low risk of early-onset posttransplant infections<br><br><br> |
| Disadvantages | <br><br>* High-risk of early-onset posttransplant infections<br><br>* No <u>graft-versus-tumor effect</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Moderate to high risk of <u>GvHD</u> and late posttransplant infection<br><br>* Increased risk of <u>graft rejection</u><br><br>* Can cause <u>chromosomal abnormalities</u> on <u>FISH</u> analysis of peripheral blood or <u>bone marrow</u> after transplant, leading to discrepancy between <u>genotype</u> and <u>phenotype</u> (e.g., if the donated <u>stem cells</u> are from a sex-mismatched donor)<br><br><br> |





### Procedure



1. * Preparation of a <u>hematopoietic stem cell</u> graft from the donor using <u>bone marrow aspirate</u>, peripheral blood, or <u>umbilical cord</u> blood
2. * Transplant preparative regimen: recipient preparation using <u>high-dose chemotherapy</u> and/or <u>total body irradiation</u>

* Rationale

* To eradicate the underlying disease

* To prevent <u>graft rejection</u> in the setting of <u>allogeneic HSCT</u>

* Regimens

* <u>Severe combined immunodeficiency</u>: No recipient preparation is required.

* <u>Aplastic anemia</u>: antithymocyte globulin and high-dose <u>cyclophosphamide</u>

* <u>Thalassemia</u>, <u>sickle cell anemia</u>: antithymocyte globulin, high-dose <u>cyclophosphamide</u>, and <u>busulfan</u>

* Malignancies: various combinations of <u>total body irradiation</u>, antithymocyte globulin, <u>cyclophosphamide</u>, <u>busulfan</u>, <u>melphalan</u>, thiotepa, <u>carmustine</u>, and <u>etoposide</u>
3. * Intravenous injection of the harvested <u>hematopoietic stem cells</u>
4. * Stem cell engraftment: anatomical and functional incorporation of transfused <u>hematopoietic stem cells</u> in the recipient's <u>bone marrow</u>

* Factors that affect the success rate of <u>engraftment</u>

* Earlier <u>engraftment</u>

* A myeloid growth factor (e.g., <u>G-CSF</u>, <u>GM-CSF</u>) may be used to accelerate <u>stem cell engraftment</u> by 3–5 days.

* <u>Peripheral blood stem cell transplant</u>

* Delayed <u>engraftment</u>

* <u>Methotrexate</u>, which is used to prevent <u>GvHD</u>, delays <u>stem cell engraftment</u> by 3–5 days.

* <u>Umbilical cord</u> <u>stem cell</u> transplant

* Confirmation

* Increase in <u>granulocyte</u> count beyond > 500/Î¼L

* <u>FISH</u> or analysis of STNRs after <u>PCR</u>: evidence of <u>chimerism</u> in peripheral <u>leukocytes</u>
5. * In <u>allogeneic stem cell transplantation</u>: regimen to prevent <u>GvHD</u>




### Complications




#### Engraftment syndrome [[35]](/library/2ZcTaa0)




* Definition: a clinical syndrome characterized by <u>fever</u>, <u>rash</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>, and/or, in more severe cases, organ dysfunction

* Etiopathogenesis

* Poorly understood; associated with <u>HSCT</u>

* Thought to be mediated by the release of <u>proinflammatory cytokines</u> (e.g., <u>IL-2</u>, <u>IL-6</u>, <u>TNF-α</u>, <u>interferon-γ</u>), <u>erythropoietin</u>, and products of <u>neutrophil</u> <u>degranulation</u> and oxidative metabolism; involves systemic <u>endothelial</u> damage

* Clinical features: develops within the first 3–4 days of <u>engraftment</u>

* <u>Fever</u>, <u>skin</u> <u>rash</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>

* Transient <u>encephalopathy</u>

* <u>Pulmonary edema</u>, <u>hypoxia</u>, weight gain

* Diagnostics: <u>clinical diagnosis</u>

* Differential diagnoses

* Acute and hyperacute <u>GvHD</u>, preengraftment syndrome, <u>hematopoietic</u> <u>graft rejection</u>

* Drug/radiation-induced toxicity

* <u>Sepsis</u>

* Treatment: depends on severity, but mainly involves <u>corticosteroids</u> (e.g., <u>methylprednisolone</u>, <u>prednisolone</u>), supportive measures (e.g., <u>antipyretics</u>, <u>diuretics</u>), and cardiovascular support (e.g., <u>intubation</u> and <u>mechanical ventilation</u>)

* Complications: hepatic and renal dysfunction

* Prognosis: highly variable, ranging from spontaneous resolution to fatal outcomes

* Prevention: limited data suggest that <u>G-CSF</u> avoidance and use of prophylactic <u>corticosteroids</u> can decrease ES <u>incidence</u> [[36]](/library/jZc_Ya0)





#### Other




* Graft failure 

* <u>Primary graft failure</u>: <u>stem cell engraftment</u> failure

* Secondary graft failure: graft failure after <u>stem cell engraftment</u>

* <u>GvHD</u>

* <u>Immunosuppression</u>-related complications

* Posttransplant infections

* <u>Posttransplant malignancy</u>





> [!TIP]
> The <u>mortality rate</u> of <u>allogeneic stem cell transplantation</u> is declining but is still as high as 50%.




> [!TIP]
> When considering a regimen to prevent <u>GvHD</u> following <u>allogeneic HSCT</u> for hematological malignancies, the risk of <u>GvHD</u> should always be weighed against the loss of a beneficial <u>graft-vs-tumor effect</u> and the risk of graft failure due to drug toxicity.

---

## Complications

Complications after transplantation can be divided into graft-related (<u>graft rejection</u>, <u>graft-versus-host disease</u>) and <u>immunosuppression</u>-related complications (infection, <u>malignancy</u>).



We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Graft rejection

### Overview



* Definition: graft failure resulting from damage by the recipient's <u>immune response</u>




| Types of graft rejection |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | <u>Hyperacute rejection</u> | <u>Acute rejection</u> | <u>Chronic rejection</u> |
| Onset | <br>* < 48 hours after transplantation, usually within minutes to hours<br><br> | <br>* < 6 months after transplantation, usually within weeks to months<br><br> | <br>* > 6 months after transplantation, usually after a few years<br><br> |
| Clinical features | <br>* Organ swelling upon <u>perfusion</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Pain</u> in the graft region<br><br>* Graft <u>edema</u><br><br>* <u>Fever</u> and deterioration of general condition<br><br><br> | <br>* Slow, progressive loss of organ function<br><br> |
| <u>Biopsy</u> | <br>* Small vessel <u>thrombosis</u> → <u>ischemia</u> → graft <u>necrosis</u><br><br> | <br>* Dense <u>interstitial</u> <u>lymphocytic</u> infiltrate with <u>vasculitis</u><br><br> | <br>* Mainly <u>arteriosclerosis</u><br><br> |
| Treatment | <br>* Graft removal<br><br> | <br>* <u>Immunosuppressive therapy</u><br><br> | <br>* Graft removal<br><br> |
| Prevention | <br>* Preoperative <u>crossmatching</u> and ABO grouping<br><br> | <br><br>* Preoperative <u>crossmatching</u> and ABO grouping<br><br>* Preoperative <u>HLA</u> matching (see “<u>Histocompatibility</u>”)<br><br>* <u>Posttransplant immunosuppressive therapy</u><br><br><br> | <br>* N/A<br><br> |










#### Hyperacute rejection




* Frequency: < 1% of posttransplant organ dysfunction

* Onset: < 48 hours after transplantation (usually within minutes to hours)

* <u>Risk factors</u>: <u>ABO incompatibility</u>, <u>HLA</u> incompatibility [[37]](/library/ojY0Y6)

* Pathophysiology

* <u>Humoral</u> rejection (<u>type II hypersensitivity reaction</u>): recipient's preformed cytotoxic <u>antibodies</u> against donor's <u>class I HLA</u> molecules or <u>blood group</u> <u>antigens</u> → activation of the <u>complement system</u> and adhesion to cells → <u>thrombosis</u> of vessels → graft <u>ischemia</u> and <u>necrosis</u>

* Preformed <u>antibodies</u> against <u>HLA</u> <u>antigens</u> result from exposure to foreign <u>HLA</u> haplotypes during <u>pregnancy</u>, <u>transfusion</u>, or a previously rejected transplant.

* Clinical features: swelling of the organ as soon as <u>perfusion</u> is restored during transplantation

* Diagnostics: small vessel <u>thrombosis</u>, <u>ischemia</u>, and graft <u>necrosis</u> on <u>biopsy</u>

* Treatment: graft removal

* Prevention: preoperative <u>crossmatching</u> and ABO grouping





![Acute transplant rejection](media/ch5nx5x86g1a22a6l1zjbdcc.jpg)

Acute transplant rejection




#### Acute rejection




* Frequency: ∼ 50% of posttransplant organ dysfunction

* Onset: < 6 months after transplantation (usually within weeks to months)

* <u>Risk factors</u>: <u>HLA</u> incompatibility, inadequate <u>immunosuppression</u>, or patient nonadherence [[37]](/library/ojY0Y6)

* Pathophysiology

* <u>Allorecognition</u> → <u>T lymphocyte</u> induced cell-mediated and/or <u>humoral immunity</u>

* Acute cellular rejection (<u>type IV hypersensitivity reaction</u>)

* Donor <u>MHC class II</u> <u>antigens</u> react with recipient <u>CD4+ T cells</u>, which then differentiate into <u>Th1</u> helper <u>T cells</u> → <u>cytokine</u> (INF-γ) release → <u>macrophage</u> recruitment → <u>parenchymal</u> and <u>endothelial</u> inflammation

* Donor <u>MHC class I</u> <u>antigens</u> react with recipient <u>CD8+ T cells</u> → direct cytotoxic cell damage

* Acute humoral rejection (<u>type II hypersensitivity reaction</u>): recipient <u>antibodies</u>, formed before or after transplantation, react against donor <u>HLA</u> <u>antigens</u>

* Clinical features

* <u>Pain</u> in the graft region

* Graft <u>edema</u>

* <u>Fever</u> and deterioration of general condition

* Diagnostics

* <u>Screening test</u>: serial organ function tests to assess for a decline in organ function

* <u>Biopsy</u> (<u>confirmatory test</u>) 

* Dense <u>interstitial</u> <u>lymphocytic</u> infiltrate with <u>vasculitis</u>

* Heterogenous mononuclear aggregates with or without <u>antibody</u> deposition

* Positive C4d staining indicates <u>humoral</u> <u>graft rejection</u>.  [[38]](/library/N7X-Nz)

* Negative <u>C4d</u> staining indicates cellular rejection.

* Treatment: Adjust dosage or regimen of <u>immunosuppressive therapy</u>. 

* <u>Acute cellular rejection</u>

* First-line: high-dose <u>glucocorticoids</u>

* Second-line: <u>lymphocyte</u>-depleting <u>antibodies</u> or OKT3 (muromonab or anti-<u>T-cell</u> <u>antibody</u>)

* <u>Acute humoral rejection</u>

* First-line

* <u>Plasmapheresis</u>

* IVIG

* Anti-<u>CD20</u> <u>antibodies</u>

* <u>Lymphocyte</u> depleting <u>antibody</u>

* <u>Corticosteroids</u> may be used as an adjunct.

* Prevention

* Preoperative <u>crossmatching</u> and ABO grouping

* Preoperative <u>HLA</u> matching (see “<u>Histocompatibility</u>”)

* <u>Posttransplant immunosuppressive therapy</u>





#### Chronic rejection




* Frequency: ∼ 50% of posttransplant organ dysfunction

* Onset: > 6 months after transplantation (usually after a few years)

* <u>Risk factors</u> [[37]](/library/ojY0Y6)

* Previous episode of <u>acute rejection</u>

* Poor <u>HLA</u> match

* Prolonged <u>cold ischemia time</u>

* <u>Hyperlipidemia</u>

* Inadequate <u>immunosuppression</u> or patient nonadherence

* Pathophysiology

* Combination of <u>humoral</u> rejection (<u>type II hypersensitivity reaction</u>) and cellular rejection (<u>type IV hypersensitivity reaction</u>)

* Donor <u>MHC class II</u> <u>antigens</u> react with recipient <u>CD4+ T cells</u> → differentiation into <u>Th1</u> helper <u>T cells</u> → <u>cytokine</u> (INF-γ) release → <u>macrophage</u> recruitment → <u>parenchymal</u> and <u>endothelial</u> inflammation

* Clinical features: slow, progressive loss of organ function

* Diagnostics

* <u>Biopsy</u>: mainly <u>arteriosclerosis</u>

* <u>Interstitial</u> <u>fibrosis</u>

* Obstruction of vessels

* Vascular <u>smooth muscle</u> <u>proliferation</u>

* Graft <u>atrophy</u> [[3]](/library/v3YA4K)

* Organ-specific manifestations

* <u>Glomerular</u> <u>sclerosis</u> (<u>kidneys</u>)

* Accelerated <u>coronary artery disease</u> (<u>heart</u>)

* <u>Vanishing bile duct syndrome</u> (<u>liver</u>)

* <u>Bronchiolitis obliterans</u> (<u>lung</u>)

* Treatment: Graft removal

* Prevention: Irreversible process with no known prevention





> [!TIP]
> <u>Graft rejection</u> manifests with organ failure and is very difficult to distinguish from other posttransplant complications. A <u>biopsy</u> is required to confirm the diagnosis.




![Chronic transplant rejection in kidney](media/s3jppihfb6cy06qirlva03n3.jpg)

Chronic transplant rejection in kidney

---

## Graft-versus-host disease (GvHD)

### Overview




* Definition: an immunological response that occurs when donor <u>T lymphocytes</u> in the graft recognize the recipient as foreign, resulting in a systemic inflammatory reaction

* Etiology

* <u>Graft-versus-host disease</u> (<u>GvHD</u>) is common in transplantation of <u>lymphocyte</u>-rich organs, including:

* <u>Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation</u>

* <u>Transfusion</u> of nonirradiated <u>blood products</u>

* <u>Small bowel</u> transplantation

* <u>HLA</u> mismatch (especially <u>HLA</u>-A, <u>HLA</u>-B, and <u>HLA-DR</u>) is associated with an increased risk of <u>GvHD</u>.

* Classification [[39]](/library/SWWyk40)

* Acute: presence of <u>acute GvHD</u> clinical features (previously defined as onset ≤ 100 days after transplantation)

* Classic acute: ≤ 100 days after transplantation

* Persistent, recurrent, or late-onset <u>acute GvHD</u>: > 100 days after transplantation

* Chronic: presence of <u>chronic GvHD</u> clinical features regardless of time of onset (previously defined as onset > 100 days after transplantation)

* Classic <u>chronic GvHD</u>: Only <u>chronic GvHD</u> features are present.

* Overlap syndrome: Both acute and <u>chronic GvHD</u> features are present.





| Types of <u>GvHD</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <u>Acute GvHD</u> | <u>Chronic GvHD</u> |
| Main affected organs | <br><br>* <u>Skin</u><br><br>* <u>Gastrointestinal tract</u><br><br>* <u>Liver</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Skin</u><br><br>* <u>Gastrointestinal tract</u><br><br>* <u>Liver</u><br><br>* <u>Lungs</u><br><br>* Eyes, mouth, <u>joints</u>, and <u>fascia</u> are affected in nearly 50% of patients<br><br><br> |
| Diagnostics | <br>* ↑ <u>ALP</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Spirometry</u>: <u>obstructive lung disease</u><br><br> |
| <br>* <u>Confirmatory test</u>: <u>biopsy</u> of the affected organ<br><br> |  |  |
| <br>Treatment [[40]](/library/VSaGAP) | <br><br>* Optimize <u>GvHD</u> prophylaxis (e.g., <u>cyclosporine</u> levels)<br><br>* Topical and/or <u>systemic corticosteroids</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* First-line: <u>corticosteroids</u><br><br>* Second-line: <u>cyclosporine</u> and increased <u>corticosteroid</u> dose<br><br><br> |










#### Acute GvHD




* <u>Epidemiology</u>: <u>Incidence</u> with prophylaxis is 9–50%; <u>incidence</u> without prophylaxis is 70–100%.

* Pathophysiology: Donor <u>T lymphocytes</u> trigger a <u>type IV hypersensitivity reaction</u> in the recipient organs, leading to severe organ damage.

* Clinical features

* Pruritic and/or painful <u>maculopapular rash</u> (involves the <u>ears</u>, nape of the neck, shoulder, soles, and palms)

* Gastrointestinal upset

* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>

* Cramping abdominal <u>pain</u>

* Hepatic dysfunction: <u>jaundice</u>, <u>hepatosplenomegaly</u>

* In rare cases: <u>lagophthalmos</u>, hemorrhagic <u>conjunctivitis</u>, <u>conjunctival</u> pseudomembrane formation

* Diagnostics

* <u>Anemia</u>, <u>thrombocytopenia</u>, <u>leukopenia</u>

* ↑ <u>ALP</u>

* <u>Confirmatory test</u>: <u>biopsy</u> of <u>skin</u>, <u>rectum</u>, or <u>liver</u> shows cell <u>apoptosis</u>, <u>endothelial</u> damage, and <u>lymphocytic</u> infiltration

* <u>Skin</u>: damaged <u>epidermis</u> and <u>hair follicles</u>

* <u>Liver</u>: segmental disruption of small <u>bile</u> ducts

* Intestines: disruption of crypts, <u>mucosal</u> <u>ulceration</u>

* Treatment [[40]](/library/VSaGAP)

* Optimize <u>GvHD</u> prophylaxis (e.g., <u>cyclosporine</u> levels)

* < 50% <u>Skin</u> involvement: <u>topical steroids</u>

* Involvement of the <u>GI tract</u>, <u>liver</u>, or > 50% of <u>skin</u>: systemic <u>steroids</u> and/or <u>topical steroids</u>

* <u>Octreotide</u> to control severe <u>diarrhea</u>

* Prevention

* <u>Irradiated</u> <u>blood products</u> (for <u>immunocompromised individuals</u>)

* Antithymocyte globulin

* <u>Cyclosporine</u> PLUS one of the following:

* <u>Methotrexate</u>

* <u>Mycophenolate mofetil</u>





#### Chronic GvHD [[39]](/library/SWWyk40)




* <u>Epidemiology</u>: ∼ 40% of patients following <u>allogeneic stem cell transplantation</u>

* Pathophysiology: Mostly unknown

* Clinical features

* Any organ can be affected.

* Pruritic <u>maculopapular rash</u>

* <u>Sicca syndrome</u>

* Chronic enteritis: bloody <u>diarrhea</u>, abdominal <u>pain</u>, weight loss

* Hepatic dysfunction: <u>jaundice</u>

* Bronchiolitis obliterans: <u>chronic cough</u>, <u>wheezing</u>, <u>dyspnea</u>

* Myasthenic symptoms

* <u>Polymyositis</u>

* <u>Scleroderma</u>-like and lichenoid <u>skin</u> changes

* <u>Fasciitis</u>

* Diagnostics

* <u>Spirometry</u>: <u>obstructive lung disease</u>

* <u>Confirmatory test</u>: <u>biopsy</u> of the <u>skin</u>, <u>oral cavity</u>, <u>liver</u>, or <u>lung</u>

* Treatment [[40]](/library/VSaGAP)

* First-line: <u>corticosteroids</u>

* Second-line : <u>cyclosporine</u> and increased <u>corticosteroid</u> dose

* Prevention: same as for <u>acute GvHD</u>





> [!TIP]
> The <u>skin</u>, intestines, and <u>liver</u> are the most commonly affected organs in <u>GvHD</u>.

---

## Immunosuppression-related complications

### Infection




| Overview of posttransplant infections |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Time of onset |  | Infection |
| <br>Early onset (< 1 month after transplantation)<br> |  | <br><br>* <u>Surgical site infections</u><br><br>* Other <u>hospital-acquired infections</u> (e.g., <u>nosocomial urinary tract infection</u>)<br><br>* <u>Candidiasis</u> (caused by non-albicans species)<br><br>* <u>C. difficile</u><br><br>* <u>Strongyloidiasis</u> [[41]](/library/ZddZoK0)<br><br><br> |
| Late onset | 1–6 months | <br><br>* <u>HHV-6</u>, <u>HHV-7</u><br><br>* <u>HSV</u><br><br>* <u>Aspergillosis</u><br><br>* <u>Strongyloidiasis</u> [[41]](/library/ZddZoK0)<br><br><br> |
| 6–12 months | <br><br>* Viral infections<br><br>* <u>CMV</u><br><br>* <u>HSV</u><br><br>* <u>VZV</u><br><br>* <u>EBV</u><br><br>* <u>Adenovirus</u><br><br>* <u>BK polyomavirus</u><br><br>* <u>Hepatitis B</u> and <u>hepatitis C</u> <u>viruses</u><br><br>* <u>Pneumocystis carinii</u> <u>pneumonia</u><br><br>* <u>Listeriosis</u><br><br>* <u>Nocardiosis</u><br><br>* <u>Strongyloidiasis</u> [[41]](/library/ZddZoK0)<br><br><br> |  |
| > 12 months | <br><br>* Viral infections<br><br>* <u>CMV</u><br><br>* <u>HSV</u><br><br>* <u>VZV</u><br><br>* <u>EBV</u> leading to <u>posttransplant lymphoproliferative disease</u><br><br>* JC <u>polyomavirus</u><br><br>* <u>HPV</u><br><br>* <u>Tuberculosis</u><br><br>* Invasive <u>fungal infections</u><br><br>* <u>Aspergillosis</u><br><br>* <u>Coccidioidomycosis</u><br><br>* <u>Histoplasmosis</u><br><br>* <u>Cryptococcal meningitis</u><br><br>* <u>Blastomycosis</u><br><br>* <u>Strongyloidiasis</u> [[41]](/library/ZddZoK0)<br><br><br> |  |





### Posttransplant malignancy




* <u>Incidence</u>: 0.4% following organ transplantation

* Common malignancies

* <u>Non-Hodgkin lymphoma</u>

* <u>Nonmelanoma skin cancer</u> (especially <u>squamous cell carcinoma</u>)

* <u>Kaposi sarcoma</u>

* <u>Hepatocellular carcinoma</u>

* Anal or <u>vulval carcinoma</u>
